explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Aaron, Moses' brother, tells them, "Take off the gold earrings that are on your wives and sons and daughters, and bring them to me." (Exodus 32:2) Then all the people take off their gold earrings and bring them to him. Whole families, and every ear got lighter.

Sandals would've been a whole different scene, friend. The camp would be hopping around barefoot, and I would've felt that in my gold base. But Aaron asks for gold earrings, the ones on their wives and sons and daughters (Exodus 32:2).

Cloaks would've left a lot of people standing around chilly and confused, baker. That's not what Aaron asks for. He says, "Take off the gold earrings that are on your wives and sons and daughters, and bring them to me." (Exodus 32:2) It's gold, and it's earrings.

A calf, baker. Aaron takes the gold from their hands, and with an engraving tool he fashions it into a molten calf (Exodus 32:4). Molten means the gold was melted and poured, then shaped. Then the people say, "These, O Israel, are your gods…"

A cherub sounds fancy, friend, but that's not what comes out of Aaron's hands. The text says he fashions the gold into a molten calf (Exodus 32:4). A calf, with an engraving tool doing the detail work. The people then say, "These, O Israel, are your gods…"

A lampstand would at least be useful, baker. But Exodus 32:4 says Aaron fashioned the gold into a molten calf. He used an engraving tool to do it. The people then announce, "These, O Israel, are your gods…"

An altar, baker. When Aaron sees the calf, he builds an altar before it and proclaims, "Tomorrow shall be a feast to the LORD." (Exodus 32:5) The next day they offer burnt offerings and present peace offerings. Things are moving fast down in that camp.

A tent would be a cozy choice, friend, but no. Exodus 32:5 says Aaron built an altar before the calf. Then he proclaimed a feast for the next day. Altars are for offerings, and offerings are exactly what they bring (Exodus 32:6).
A wall, baker? That's a lot of bricklaying for one evening. The text says Aaron built an altar before the calf (Exodus 32:5). Then he proclaimed, "Tomorrow shall be a feast to the LORD."

True, baker. The next day they offer burnt offerings and present peace offerings. Then "the people sat down to eat and drink and got up to indulge in revelry." (Exodus 32:6) Meanwhile, up on the mountain, God is about to speak to Moses.

This one is actually true, friend. After the offerings, the text says "the people sat down to eat and drink and got up to indulge in revelry." (Exodus 32:6) They offered burnt offerings and presented peace offerings first. Then came the eating, the drinking and the revelry.

Quickly, baker. The LORD says, "How quickly they have turned aside from the way that I commanded them!" (Exodus 32:8) He lists it out: they made a molten calf, bowed down to it and sacrificed to it. Moses had been gone a while, but the turning aside happened FAST.

Slowly is the opposite, friend. The LORD says, "How quickly they have turned aside from the way that I commanded them!" (Exodus 32:8) He's pointing at how fast it happened. They made the calf, bowed down to it and sacrificed to it.

Nothing in the text calls it secret, baker. The LORD's word for it is "quickly." He says, "How quickly they have turned aside from the way that I commanded them!" (Exodus 32:8) They made a molten calf, bowed down to it and sacrificed to it.

Not quite, baker. The text says the opposite: "But Moses sought the favor of the LORD his God." (Exodus 32:11) The LORD had just said, "Now leave Me alone…" and Moses answers with a plea for the people. He asks why the LORD's anger burns against His people, whom He brought out of Egypt.

False is right, baker. Right after "Now leave Me alone," the text says Moses "sought the favor of the LORD his God." (Exodus 32:11) He speaks up and asks why the LORD's anger burns against His people. I think that's a man who really cares about the people he leads.

explanations.answer: He brought them out to kill them in the mountains
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Moses asks, "Why should the Egyptians declare, 'He brought them out with evil intent, to kill them in the mountains and wipe them from the face of the earth'?" (Exodus 32:12) Then he asks the LORD to turn from His fierce anger and relent from doing harm to His people. Moses is pleading for them.

explanations.answer: Their own gods had beaten the God of Israel
explanations.explanation: That's not what Moses says, friend. The Egyptians in his words are saying, "He brought them out with evil intent, to kill them in the mountains and wipe them from the face of the earth." (Exodus 32:12) It's about evil intent and the mountains. Moses then asks the LORD to relent from doing harm.

explanations.answer: Moses tricked the people into leaving Egypt
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't put himself in that line, baker. He says the Egyptians might declare, "He brought them out with evil intent, to kill them in the mountains and wipe them from the face of the earth." (Exodus 32:12) Notice the "He" there. He's talking about the LORD, and asking Him to turn from His fierce anger.

explanations.answer: Descendants like the stars and the land
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Moses reminds the LORD of what He declared: "I will make your descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky, and I will give your descendants all this land that I have promised, and it shall be their inheritance forever." (Exodus 32:13) Moses brings up the promise itself. That's a man who knows what to hold onto.

explanations.answer: A temple on this very mountain
explanations.explanation: A temple isn't in the promise Moses quotes, friend. He says the LORD swore to make their descendants "as numerous as the stars in the sky," and to give them "all this land that I have promised." (Exodus 32:13) Descendants and land, that's the pair.

Egypt isn't the land in the promise, baker. Moses quotes the LORD: "I will give your descendants all this land that I have promised, and it shall be their inheritance forever." (Exodus 32:13) Before that, He promises descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky.

True, baker. The text says, "So the LORD relented from the calamity He had threatened to bring on His people." (Exodus 32:14) That comes right after Moses pleads for them and reminds the LORD of His promise to Abraham, Isaac and Israel. The calamity doesn't come.

This one is true, friend. After Moses pleads, "the LORD relented from the calamity He had threatened to bring on His people." (Exodus 32:14) The plea came first, then the relenting. It's a good verse to keep in the pantry.

Singing, baker. Joshua, Moses' assistant, says, "The sound of war is in the camp." But Moses replies, "It is neither the cry of victory nor the cry of defeat; I hear the sound of singing!" (Exodus 32:17-18) Joshua heard war, and Moses heard something else. I think Joshua was about to get a very different kind of news.

Moses says it's not that one, friend. His words are, "It is neither the cry of victory nor the cry of defeat; I hear the sound of singing!" (Exodus 32:18) He crosses off both war cries. Singing is what he hears.

Close, but Moses crosses that one out too, baker. He says, "It is neither the cry of victory nor the cry of defeat; I hear the sound of singing!" (Exodus 32:18) Joshua, Moses' assistant, had said war. Moses says singing.

Not this time, baker. The text says Moses "burned with anger and threw the tablets out of his hands, shattering them at the base of the mountain." (Exodus 32:19) He doesn't hand them to anybody. Joshua, Moses' assistant, was walking with him, but the tablets break.

False is right, baker. When Moses sees the calf and the dancing, he "burned with anger and threw the tablets out of his hands, shattering them at the base of the mountain." (Exodus 32:19) No handoff, no safekeeping. The tablets were the work of God, and they break right there (Exodus 32:16).

Drink, baker. Moses burned the calf, ground it to powder and scattered the powder over the water. Then, the text says, "he forced the Israelites to drink it." (Exodus 32:20) It's a heavy moment, and it shows how seriously Moses took what they had made.
Burying isn't in the text, friend. Moses burns the calf, grinds it to powder and scatters the powder over the water. Then "he forced the Israelites to drink it." (Exodus 32:20)

Watching would've been the easy part, baker. But the text says Moses scattered the powder over the face of the water. Then "he forced the Israelites to drink it." (Exodus 32:20) They had to do more than watch.

Evil, baker. Aaron says, "Do not be enraged, my lord. You yourself know that the people are intent on evil." (Exodus 32:22) That's his answer when Moses asks what the people did to him to lead them into so great a sin. I think Aaron was reaching for any answer he could find.

Leaving isn't what Aaron says, friend. His words are, "You yourself know that the people are intent on evil." (Exodus 32:22) He's answering Moses' question about leading the people into so great a sin.
Peace would've been a calmer thing to say, baker. But Aaron tells Moses, "You yourself know that the people are intent on evil." (Exodus 32:22) He says it right after telling Moses not to be enraged.

Not quite, baker. Aaron does repeat what the people asked for. But then he says, "So I said to them, 'Whoever has gold, let him take it off,' and they gave it to me. And when I threw it into the fire, out came this calf!" (Exodus 32:24) The engraving tool doesn't come up in his words to Moses. Earlier, the text says Aaron fashioned the gold with an engraving tool (Exodus 32:4).

False is right, baker. Aaron repeats the people's request, then tells Moses, "And when I threw it into the fire, out came this calf!" (Exodus 32:24) He never mentions an engraving tool or fashioning it himself. The earlier verse says he did use one (Exodus 32:4).

The Levites, baker. Moses stands at the entrance to the camp and says, "Whoever is for the LORD, come to me." The text says, "And all the Levites gathered around him." (Exodus 32:26) All of them came.
The elders aren't named here, friend. After Moses calls, "Whoever is for the LORD, come to me," the text says, "And all the Levites gathered around him." (Exodus 32:26) It's the Levites who come.

Judah isn't mentioned in this moment, baker. When Moses calls, "Whoever is for the LORD, come to me," the text says, "And all the Levites gathered around him." (Exodus 32:26) The Levites are the ones who answer.

True, baker. Moses says to the Levites, "Today you have been ordained for service to the LORD, since each man went against his son and his brother; so the LORD has bestowed a blessing on you this day." (Exodus 32:29) It comes after a heavy day. I think this part of the story is hard to sit with.

This one is true, friend. Moses tells the Levites, "…so the LORD has bestowed a blessing on you this day." (Exodus 32:29) He says it right after telling them they've been ordained for service to the LORD. It's a hard day, and a blessing is named in the middle of it.

explanations.answer: To be blotted out of God's book
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Moses says, "Yet now, if You would only forgive their sin.... But if not, please blot me out of the book that You have written." (Exodus 32:32) He puts himself on the line for the people. I think that tells you how much he cares for them.

explanations.answer: To be released from leading them
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't ask to step down, friend. He says, "If You would only forgive their sin.... But if not, please blot me out of the book that You have written." (Exodus 32:32) He asks for forgiveness for the people first.

explanations.answer: To be given a new people to lead
explanations.explanation: A new people isn't his request, baker. The LORD had offered to make Moses into a great nation (Exodus 32:10), but Moses pleads for these people instead. He says, "But if not, please blot me out of the book that You have written." (Exodus 32:32)

Sinned, baker. The LORD replies to Moses, "Whoever has sinned against Me, I will blot out of My book." (Exodus 32:33) It's His answer to Moses' request about being blotted out of the book. Then He tells Moses to go lead the people to the place He described.
Complaining isn't the word, friend. The LORD says, "Whoever has sinned against Me, I will blot out of My book." (Exodus 32:33) He's answering Moses' request about the book. The word is sinned.
Fighting isn't the word here, baker. The LORD says, "Whoever has sinned against Me, I will blot out of My book." (Exodus 32:33) He's replying to Moses' request in verse 32.

Not this time, baker. The LORD tells Moses, "Now go, lead the people to the place I described." (Exodus 32:34) Moses isn't told to stay put on the mountain while they wait. He's told to go and lead them.

False is right, baker. The LORD says, "Now go, lead the people to the place I described. Behold, My angel shall go before you." (Exodus 32:34) Moses is sent to lead the people, with the LORD's angel going before them. No waiting around on the mountain.
